adam-smith: Adam Smith (1723–1790) was a Scottish Enlightenment philosopher and economist, author of The Wealth of Nations and The Theory of Moral Sentiments. He is best known for the invisible hand, the idea that self-interested market activity can unintentionally serve the public good, and for the impartial spectator, the internalized observer by which we judge our own conduct.
annette-baier: Annette Baier was a New Zealand-born analytic philosopher and leading interpreter of David Hume who spent much of her career in North America. She is especially associated with the ethics of care and with arguing that trust, rather than detached rational contract, is the foundation of morality and of personhood.
augustine: Augustine of Hippo (354–430) was a North African bishop and the most influential philosopher of early Christianity, bridging classical and medieval thought. His Confessions and City of God shaped Western thinking on the problem of evil, free will, the nature of time, and the divided will that wants what it also rejects.
bentham: Jeremy Bentham (1748–1832) was an English radical reformer and the founder of utilitarianism, holding that actions are right insofar as they maximize pleasure and minimize pain. He designed the famous hedonic calculus for measuring happiness and also proposed the Panopticon, a prison design later made a symbol of surveillance.
confucius: Confucius (551–479 BC) was a Chinese teacher and advisor whose sayings, collected in the Analects, founded the Confucian tradition that shaped East Asian civilization. He emphasized ren (benevolence), li (ritual propriety), and xiao (filial piety), holding that a good society grows out of cultivated relationships rather than abstract rules.
cornel-west: Cornel West (b. 1953) is an American philosopher, critic, and public intellectual who works in the pragmatist tradition of Emerson, Dewey, and Du Bois. He is known for bringing that tradition to bear on race, democracy, and popular culture, arguing for a prophetic, justice-oriented democratic way of life.
darwin: Charles Darwin was a nineteenth-century English naturalist whose theory of evolution by natural selection transformed philosophy as much as biology. By showing humans to be continuous with other animals, he unsettled fixed views of human nature, design, morality, and the place of mind in the natural world.
dogen: Dogen (1200–1253) was a Japanese Buddhist monk who founded the Soto school of Zen after studying in China. His dense, poetic writings in the Shobogenzo treat meditation practice, impermanence, and non-self as inseparable, teaching that enlightenment is not attained at some future moment but enacted in present activity.
epictetus: Epictetus (c. 50–135 AD) was a Greek Stoic who began life as a slave and taught philosophy in Rome and Nicopolis; his oral teaching survives as the Discourses and the Enchiridion. He is best known for the dichotomy of control: some things are up to us (judgment, desire) and some are not, and freedom lies in wanting only the former.
hooks: bell hooks (1952–2021), the pen name (lowercase by choice) of Gloria Jean Watkins, was an American feminist theorist and cultural critic. Writing accessibly for a broad public, she reframed feminism as a movement to end sexist oppression for everyone, and connected race, class, gender, and the politics of love.
j-l-austin: J.L. Austin was a twentieth-century British ordinary-language philosopher who led the linguistic-philosophy movement at Oxford. In How to Do Things with Words he showed that utterances do not merely describe the world: with speech acts such as promising or naming, saying something is itself a way of doing something.
kristeva: Julia Kristeva is a Bulgarian-French philosopher, psychoanalyst, and literary theorist who became prominent in postwar Paris alongside the poststructuralists. She is best known for the concept of abjection, the uneasy response to what disturbs the boundary between self and other, and for work linking language, the body, and the unconscious.
lucretius: Lucretius (c. 99–55 BC) was a Roman poet whose epic De Rerum Natura expounds the atomism and ethics of Epicurus. Arguing that everything, including the soul, is made of atoms, he held that death is nothing to us and that freeing ourselves from fear of gods and death opens the way to tranquility.
macintyre: Alasdair MacIntyre (b. 1929) is a Scottish-born American philosopher whose book After Virtue revitalized virtue ethics in the analytic world. He argues that moral reasoning only makes sense within traditions, practices, and a narrative account of a life, and that modern liberal moral discourse has lost that context.
marcus-aurelius: Marcus Aurelius (121–180 AD) was Roman emperor and a Stoic philosopher; his private notebooks, published as the Meditations, were never meant for an audience. In them he practices self-examination, mortality, and the view from above, modeling how Stoic discipline can be lived amid power and crisis.
nussbaum: Martha Nussbaum (b. 1947) is an American philosopher who works across ancient Greek ethics, political philosophy, and the emotions. She is best known for the capabilities approach, developed with economist Amartya Sen, which measures human flourishing by what people are actually able to do and be rather than by wealth or preference satisfaction.
ockham: William of Ockham (c. 1287–1347) was an English Franciscan friar and one of the sharpest medieval logicians and metaphysicians. His name is attached to Ockham's Razor, the principle of preferring explanations with fewer entities, and his nominalism about universals helped clear the ground for modern science and philosophy.
pascal: Blaise Pascal (1623–1662) was a French mathematician, physicist, and religious thinker who abandoned pure science for a mystical Christian faith recorded in the fragmentary Pensees. He is best known for Pascal's Wager, an argument that, where reason cannot decide God's existence, betting on belief is the rational course.
paulo-freire: Paulo Freire was a Brazilian educator and philosopher whose Pedagogy of the Oppressed became one of the most influential books in educational theory. He criticized the banking model of education, where teachers deposit information into passive students, arguing instead for dialogue that lets the oppressed read their world and change it.
peirce: Charles Sanders Peirce (1839–1914) was an American logician, scientist, and philosopher regarded as the founder of pragmatism, a movement he later renamed pragmaticism to distance it from popular misunderstandings. He developed the pragmatic method for clarifying concepts, a theory of signs, and abduction, inference to the best explanation.
rorty: Richard Rorty (1931–2007) was an American philosopher who turned from analytic philosophy to a radical, literary pragmatism in the line of Dewey and James. In Philosophy and the Mirror of Nature he argued against the idea of philosophy as foundation-finding, urging that we drop the quest for objective truth about reality and judge ideas by their usefulness for human purposes.
seneca: Seneca (c. 4 BC–65 AD) was a Roman Stoic philosopher, dramatist, and statesman who tutored the emperor Nero and died by forced suicide. His letters and essays give Stoicism a practical, psychological cast, addressing anger, grief, time, and how to live calmly with fortune's reversals.
spencer: Herbert Spencer (1820–1903) was an English polymath who applied evolution to nearly everything, coining the phrase survival of the fittest before Darwin's Origin appeared. He championed laissez-faire liberalism, and the social Darwinism attributed to him, which used evolutionary struggle to justify hierarchy, is more complicated than his reputation suggests but remains what he is remembered for.
thoreau: Henry David Thoreau (1817–1862) was an American writer and naturalist of the New England Transcendentalist movement. His two years at Walden Pond, recounted in Walden, made him a symbol of deliberate, simple living, and his essay Civil Disobedience, defending refusal to comply with unjust law, influenced Gandhi and Martin Luther King Jr.
